title: UK state fund to lend £1bn to KKR and RWE for Vanguard windfarms
content:
The UK national wealth fund is set to lend £1 billion towards the Vanguard offshore windfarm projects off the coast of Norfolk. Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the investment as a vote of confidence in building in Britain, noting that the two windfarms require almost £13 billion in debt financing. However, the article questions whether the private equity giant KKR and German utility RWE actually needed state assistance, given their financial strength.

The piece argues that the project does not represent a fresh expression of confidence, as it has been in development since RWE was awarded the contract to build the windfarms in January’s renewables auction.
summary: The UK national wealth fund will provide a £1bn loan toward the Vanguard windfams off the coast of Norfolk, which require almost £13bn in total debt financing. The article notes that the project has been in development since RWE won a renewables auction contract in January.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Labour MPs warn against weakening 2030 electric vehicle targets
content: Exclusive: Cutting 2030 goal would be a ‘step backwards’, say MPs, as ministers clash over proposed reductions Labour MPs are urging the government not to weaken its electric vehicle targets as divided cabinet ministers prepare for a crunch meeting on Thursday to thrash out a compromise. Members of the climate and nature crisis caucus (CNCC) say ministers must not water down a legal requirement for carmakers to ensure that 80% of the vehicles they sell in 2030 are electric, saying doing so would be a backward step and “shortsighted”.
summary: Labour MPs urge the government not to weaken the legal requirement for 80% of vehicles sold in 2030 to be electric. They describe cutting this goal as a backward step ahead of a cabinet meeting to resolve ministerial disagreements.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Study links frequent sleep starts to poorer sleep, higher anxiety
content: A new study published in PLOS Mental Health indicates that individuals who frequently experience sleep starts, also known as hypnic jerks, report poorer sleep quality, greater insomnia severity, and higher anxiety levels compared to those who do not. The research was conducted by Tanja Grünberger and Manuel Schabus of Paris Lodron University Salzburg, Austria, along with their colleagues.
summary: A study published in PLOS Mental Health found that people who frequently experience sleep starts report poorer sleep quality and greater insomnia severity. These individuals also reported higher anxiety levels than those who do not experience these phenomena.
author: Medical Xpress

title: CHLA researchers identify key pathway in heart lymphatic vessel development
content: Researchers at Children's Hospital Los Angeles have identified molecular signals that guide the development of the heart's lymphatic vessel network. This discovery provides new understanding of how these vessels form normally and how they react to injury.
summary: Researchers at Children's Hospital Los Angeles have uncovered molecular signals that shape the heart's lymphatic vessel network. This discovery offers new insight into the normal formation of these vessels and their response to injury.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Psychedelic aftereffects may offer a window into psychotic symptoms
content: A 25-year-old man reported experiencing nightly hallucinations of a large, unblinking eye in his ceiling, which he described as feeling as though the world was being sucked into it. Although he did not have psychosis and was not currently using drugs, he had a history of psychedelic use. Concerned about his mental health, he contacted Max Greenwald, an M.D.-Ph.D. student at Yale School of Medicine, to ask if he was developing psychosis.
summary: Every night, as he fell asleep, a 25-year-old man saw an eye in his ceiling. It was huge and unblinking, and it felt as if the whole world was being sucked into it.
author: Medical Xpress

title: ICU patients without pharmacist care for one day face 20% higher death risk
content: New research led by the University of Georgia indicates that intensive care unit patients are 20% more likely to die if they do not receive pharmacist care for at least one day during their stay. The findings were published in the journal CHEST.
summary: New research led by the University of Georgia found that intensive care unit patients are 20% more likely to die if they do not receive pharmacist care for even one day. The study was published in the journal CHEST.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Common cardiovascular biomarker may contribute to heart disease
content: Heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States, claiming a life approximately every 34 seconds. A significant driver of these fatalities is heart failure, a progressive condition characterized by the heart’s inability to pump sufficient blood throughout the body.
summary: Heart disease is the leading cause of death in the United States, claiming a life nearly every 34 seconds. A major driver of these fatalities is heart failure, a progressive condition where the heart struggles to pump enough blood throughout the body.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Urgent care imaging for low back pain linked to fewer ED advanced scans
content:
A retrospective cohort study led by Mass General Brigham researchers identifies urgent care as a promising setting for managing low back pain imaging. The study notes that low back pain contributes significantly to U.S. health care spending, meaning that even minor adjustments in imaging practices could substantially influence overall resource use.

The research analyzed 2,924 urgent care lumbar spine X-rays performed for uncomplicated low back pain. The findings indicate that only 24 of these patients underwent emergency department advanced imaging within 30 days, suggesting a limited progression to more intensive diagnostic procedures following initial urgent care evaluation.
summary: A retrospective cohort study led by Mass General Brigham researchers examined imaging practices for uncomplicated low back pain. The study found that only 24 of 2,924 urgent care lumbar spine X-rays were followed by emergency department advanced imaging within 30 days.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Postpartum psychosis not recognized as standalone DSM category
content: Postpartum psychosis has recently gained public attention following the tragic case of Lindsay Clancy, as most people had limited prior knowledge of the condition. Despite its severity, the illness is not classified as a standalone category in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM). This guidebook, published by the American Psychiatric Association, is used to classify various mental health conditions, including anxiety, depression, obsessive-compulsive, and trauma-related disorders.
summary: Postpartum psychosis gained public attention this year following the Lindsay Clancy case. The illness is not recognized as a standalone category in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Low-cost parenting app cuts sexual violence against Tanzanian adolescent girls by over 50%
content:
The study led by the University of Oxford’s Department of Social Policy and Intervention found that a digital parenting program in Tanzania cut sexual violence and exploitation of adolescent girls by more than half.  

A separate study indicates the program could also generate substantial savings for health services, presenting a potentially affordable method to prevent violence against children.
summary: The digital parenting program reduced sexual violence and exploitation among adolescent girls in Tanzania by more than half, according to research led by the University of Oxford's Department of Social Policy and Intervention. A separate study says the program could generate substantial health‑service savings, offering an affordable approach to preventing violence against children.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Elon Musk ends Cybertruck production to focus on Cybercab robotaxi
content:
Production of the Tesla Cybertruck is winding down, a development that has drawn criticism from safety campaigners and complaints from owners. The vehicle, described in the article as a "steel monstrosity" with a design likened to that of a five-year-old, is being phased out despite its polarizing reception.

Elon Musk, who recently moved from California to Texas, stated that the decision is not due to the vehicle being unprofitable, a claim he attributed to misreporting by legacy media. Instead, Musk explained via tweet that the opportunity cost associated with the Cybertruck’s complexity is outweighed by the value of producing the Cybercab, a two-passenger robotaxi. This shift in focus comes as Musk faces other challenges, including a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government during the midterms and potential legal investigations by Democrats in his newly blue state.
summary: Tesla is winding down production of the Cybertruck, a vehicle criticized by safety campaigners and owners for its design. Elon Musk stated the decision is driven by the opportunity cost of complexity, prioritizing the production of the two-passenger Cybercab robotaxi instead.
author: Guardian Business

title: Nvidia hires Wachtell to investigate Jensen Huang's relationship with alleged Chinese spy
content:
Nvidia has appointed New York-based law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between CEO Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy. The $4.1 trillion chipmaker made the move following reports that Huang was having an affair with the individual. Joon Kim, a Wachtell partner and former New York government prosecutor, will lead the inquiry.

Kim is described on the firm’s website as a specialist in internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defense, and crisis management. The appointment comes as Nvidia deals with the fallout from the allegations regarding its chief executive.
summary: Nvidia has appointed the New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a thorough and independent investigation into the relationship between CEO Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy. The investigation will be led by Wachtell partner Joon Kim, a former government prosecutor specializing in internal investigations and crisis management.
author: Guardian Business

title: Democrats' election sweep highlights fiscal reality of promised social contract
content:
The recent Democratic sweep in US elections has shifted attention to the fiscal implications of their proposed social contract. The article notes that the post-election agenda faces immediate financial constraints, stating that “there is no money” to fund the extensive list of promised programs. This fiscal reality contrasts with the political ambition of the new crop of Democrats who have taken power.

The incoming Democratic leadership is pushing for significant expansions in social support, including programs for children and parents and a strong endorsement of Medicare for All. Their platform also includes reversing specific actions taken by Donald Trump, such as restoring cuts to Medicaid and food stamps. Additionally, the group aims to reinstate health insurance subsidies under the Affordable Care Act that had previously expired due to Republican inaction.

The text frames this political shift as a potential turning point for US society, comparing it to the Reagan revolution of four decades ago. While the Reagan era moved the country toward lower taxes and reduced social solidarity, the current Democratic momentum suggests a move toward a new social contract focused on equitable prosperity. The article concludes by noting that the outlined initiatives represent only the beginning of the broader political project.
summary: The new crop of Democrats calls for support for children, Medicare for All, and restoring Medicaid and food stamp cuts. The article notes that these ambitious promises face harsh fiscal reality because there is no money.
author: Guardian Business

title: New Chip Sorts Cells via Electrical Signature and Sound Wave
content: Researchers in Singapore and China have developed a noninvasive, label-free method to sort cells using a chip that identifies them by their electrical signature and separates them with a precisely aimed sound wave. This approach addresses the limitations of current techniques, such as fluorescence-activated cell sorting, which rely on extrinsic labeling that can stress cells, alter their behavior, and interfere with assays.
summary: A collaborative study between researchers in Singapore and China developed a noninvasive, label-free method to sort cells. The technology identifies cells by their electrical signature and separates them using a precisely aimed sound wave.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists question feasibility of reviving extinct species
content: Scientists question the feasibility of de‑extinction, the idea of reviving extinct species. Recent advances in biotechnology—such as ancient DNA sequencing, genome analysis and gene editing—have prompted some to believe that extinction could one day be reversed.
summary: Scientists are challenging the dream of bringing extinct species back to life. Advances in biotechnology such as ancient DNA sequencing, genome analysis and gene editing have led some to believe it may be possible.
author: Phys.org

title: Biodegradable bubble moves away from lactic acid without a motor—a step toward artificial cells
content:
Researchers led by chemist Daniela Wilson at Radboud University, in collaboration with colleagues at Durham University, have developed a tiny biodegradable bubble capable of moving away from a chemical without a motor. This autonomous movement contrasts with living cells, which require complex molecular machinery to perform similar actions.

This discovery represents a step toward creating artificial cells with lifelike behavior. In the long term, the research could provide an interesting approach for self-steering particles in targeted drug delivery.
summary: A tiny biodegradable bubble can move away from a chemical on its own, without a motor. Living cells need complex molecular machinery to do this.
author: Phys.org

title: Penn State study finds most dryland soil microbes stay dormant after rain
content:
Researchers at Penn State have discovered that when infrequent rainfall wets dryland soil, most microbes within biological soil crusts remain inactive. These microbes typically stay dormant for long periods in arid regions, only "awakening" when they sense moisture. The study was motivated by projections indicating that these threatened ecosystems could decline by up to 40% over the next 45 years.

The findings reveal that only a subset of the microbial community responds to the moisture. According to the researchers, this discovery will inform ongoing efforts to conserve and restore biocrusts in dryland environments.
summary: Researchers at Penn State discovered that most microbes in biological soil crusts remain inactive when dryland soil receives moisture. This finding aims to inform efforts to conserve and restore these ecosystems, which are projected to decline by 40% in the next 45 years.
author: Phys.org

title: HKUST researchers find bacteria-housing structure in deep-sea mollusk
content: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have discovered a previously unknown specialized organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk living at cold seeps in the South China Sea. Dedicated to maintaining bacterial symbiosis, this newly identified survival mechanism provides new insights into how deep-sea organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments and opens new directions for research on chemosymbiosis, organelle evolution and deep-sea ecosystems.
summary: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology discovered a new organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk that houses bacteria. This finding offers insights into how organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments in the South China Sea.
author: Phys.org

title: New Scientist readers explain why music evokes emotion across cultures
content: New Scientist’s Last Word series featured a reader question asking why music evokes emotion and whether people from other cultures share these feelings. The publication shared responses from its readers, who provided scientific answers to the inquiry.
summary: New Scientist's Last Word series posed a question about why music evokes emotion and whether people from other cultures feel the same way. The publication shared the scientific answers provided by its readers to this inquiry.
author: New Scientist

title: Experts urge preservation of space age artefacts like Voyager 1
content:
The Voyager 1 probe, which began its journey nearly 50 years ago, will mark a significant milestone on 18 November by traveling one light day from Earth. It is projected to pass near the star Gliese 445 in approximately 40,000 years, continuing an endless drift that represents humanity’s first attempt to reach the stars. Unlike most iconic spacecraft that have burned up in Earth’s atmosphere or settled in the ocean, Voyager 1 has operated for the majority of the space age, making it a rare surviving artifact.

Current efforts to preserve space history are described as being in a "dark ages" phase, with little attention paid to keeping spacecraft in situ for future generations. Major assets such as the Hubble Space Telescope and the International Space Station are expected to end their lives similarly to previous missions, despite scientific calls for Hubble’s preservation. While some hardware, like the space shuttles, is displayed in museums, the Apollo equipment left on the moon lacks significant protection under international law.

To address this gap, the article suggests establishing an organization similar to the UNESCO World Heritage Committee to designate and fund the preservation of important space artifacts. Such an initiative would rely on cultural and heritage budgets rather than scientific ones. However, this approach faces challenges, including threats to these budgets and the United States’ planned departure from UNESCO at the end of the year.

As an alternative to government or institutional funding, private philanthropy is proposed as a viable option. The text draws a parallel to 19th-century industrialists like Andrew Carnegie and J. P. Morgan, who funded major cultural institutions. It suggests that lobbying for the creation of entities such as a "Musk Space Museum" or "Bezos Orbital Institute" could help ensure that humanity can look back on its origins in space exploration.
summary: The article argues that iconic spacecraft such as Voyager 1, Hubble, and the International Space Station lack adequate protection for future preservation. It suggests creating an organisation similar to UNESCO or using private philanthropy to safeguard these space age artefacts.
author: New Scientist

title: Blood-thinning drug dabigatran reduces cartilage damage and pain in osteoarthritis animal models
content:
A blood-thinning drug has demonstrated the ability to reduce pain and improve mobility in animal models of knee osteoarthritis, according to research published in Science Translational Medicine. The study, led by Chuan-Ju Liu at Yale University, found that the drug dabigatran, which is commonly used to prevent blood clots in patients at risk of strokes, also blocks inflammatory signals associated with the disease. In experiments involving monkeys and mice, the treatment resulted in reduced cartilage damage and improved joint function.

Osteoarthritis, a condition affecting more than 500 million people worldwide, is characterized by the wear and tear of cartilage that cushions bone ends, leading to inflammation, pain, and stiffness. While painkillers and anti-inflammatory drugs can manage symptoms, no currently approved medications halt or slow the worsening of the disease. Tonia Vincent at the University of Oxford, who was not involved in the study, noted that current options for patients are limited to weight loss suggestions or drugs that provide only pain relief.

The research team investigated whether targeting both TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta, two inflammatory molecules believed to drive osteoarthritis, would be more effective than targeting them individually. Previous clinical trials targeting these molecules individually have been unsuccessful, potentially because the molecules compensate for each other when one is blocked. To test this, the researchers surgically removed part of the cartilage in the left knee joints of eight monkeys to mimic the wear and tear that triggers the condition.

One month after the surgery, four of the monkeys received a daily dose of dabigatran mixed into their food, while the remaining monkeys served as controls. After seven months, MRI scans showed that the left-knee cartilage in the monkeys taking dabigatran was approximately 60 percent thicker on average compared to the control group. Additionally, the treated monkeys exhibited a roughly 15 percent greater range of motion in their left knee. Liu stated that these monkeys displayed a more natural walking pattern and greater knee movement, consistent with reduced joint stiffness and discomfort.

Further experiments in mice with surgically induced knee osteoarthritis confirmed these findings, revealing that dabigatran reduced inflammation in the knee by about 60 percent. Vincent praised the use of established animal models for osteoarthritis, suggesting that if another research group replicates the findings, a small clinical trial could be considered. However, Liu noted that it remains unclear whether the approach can reverse damage that has already occurred.

A significant limitation of using dabigatran is that reducing blood clotting increases the risk of bleeding in human patients. To address this, the researchers are developing new drugs that target TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta without affecting clotting, which they plan to test in mice before any clinical trials. Vincent also pointed out that prior studies suggest inhibiting clotting molecules might relieve osteoarthritis symptoms, meaning some of dabigatran’s benefits could stem from its anti-clotting properties rather than its anti-inflammatory effects. Further research comparing dabigatran with drugs that lack clotting effects is needed to clarify these mechanisms.
summary: Researchers found that the blood-thinning drug dabigatran reduced cartilage loss and improved mobility in monkeys and mice with knee osteoarthritis by blocking inflammatory signals TNF-alpha and IL-1-beta. The study suggests the drug could slow disease progression, though further research is needed to separate its anti-clotting effects from its anti-inflammatory benefits.
author: New Scientist

title: Paleontologists find 450-million-year-old starfish relative fossil with soft tissue
content: Scientists have identified a 450-million-year-old fossil in a museum collection that preserves soft tissues from an ancient starfish relative. This rare specimen offers new insights into how Earth’s earliest reef animals fed, survived, and evolved, providing details about marine life from a period more than 200 million years before the existence of dinosaurs.
summary: Scientists discovered a rare 450-million-year-old fossil with preserved soft tissues from an ancient starfish relative in a museum collection. The specimen provides new insights into how early reef animals fed, survived, and evolved prior to the age of dinosaurs.
author: Science Daily

title: Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth
content:
New research from the University of Cambridge challenges the century-old theory that comets delivered the ingredients for life to Earth. The study indicates that comets traveled too fast and struck at unfavorable angles, making it extraordinarily unlikely for the fragile molecules required for life to survive the impact.

While Mars may have had a slightly better chance of receiving these cosmic ingredients, the odds remained slim. The findings suggest that asteroids or chemical processes on Earth are more plausible sources for life’s building blocks.
summary: A century-old theory about the origins of life on Earth may be wrong. New research from the University of Cambridge suggests that comets traveled too fast and struck at unfavorable angles for the fragile molecules needed for life to survive, making successful delivery extraordinarily unlikely.
author: Science Daily

title: NASA Hubble Space Telescope spots 93-billion-mile dust cloud from colliding planets
content: NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope has identified a 93-billion-mile-long cloud of dark, fluffy dust that may result from collisions between massive planetary bodies. This discovery challenges prior assumptions about the structure and provides new insights into the violent formation of planetary systems.
summary: NASA's Hubble Space Telescope revealed a 93-billion-mile-long cloud of dark, fluffy dust. The cloud may have formed when massive planetary bodies collided, challenging previous assumptions and offering new clues about the violent birth of planetary systems.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find mosquito species prefer different human skin odors and bacteria
content: A new study finds that different mosquito species are drawn to distinct blends of human skin odors, chemicals and bacteria, indicating that preferences vary among species. The findings dispute the notion of a single universal mosquito attractant and suggest the potential for species‑specific repellents targeting disease‑carrying mosquitoes.
summary: The study shows each mosquito species is attracted to a unique mix of skin odors, chemicals, and bacteria. Researchers say the finding challenges the idea of a universal mosquito magnet and could aid development of more effective repellents for disease‑spreading mosquitoes.
author: Science Daily

title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
content:
Scientists have developed a bioengineered chewing gum designed to combat microbes associated with head and neck cancer. The new treatment reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples collected from cancer patients. Additionally, a single dose of the gum’s extract nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species.

The study highlights that this intervention effectively targets pathogens while sparing beneficial bacteria in the mouth. This approach offers a potential new tool for managing oral health risks linked to specific cancer-causing microbes.
summary: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract.
author: Science Daily

title: Rhiannon Adam's photo captures SpaceX Starship breakup during 2023 test flight
content:
Rhiannon Adam, a photographer selected for the dearMoon Project, shared a photograph taken on April 20, 2023, from a VIP viewing area in South Padre Island, Texas. The image captures the moment SpaceX’s Starship vehicle broke apart during its Integrated Flight Test 1. Adam was one of eight civilians chosen from an open call in 2021 to fly around the Moon on a free SpaceX Starship mission funded by Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa. The project also included another photographer, and Adam described the selection as a surreal experience that significantly altered her perception of her own worth.

The flight, originally scheduled for 2023, dominated Adam’s life, causing her to stop receiving commissions as clients assumed she was preoccupied with space travel. On the day of the test, observers watched the rocket lift off relatively successfully before the vehicle experienced an “Rapid Unscheduled Disassembly” (RUD) four minutes into the flight. The explosion created a dust cloud from the concrete launchpad and tower, with debris scattering onto local houses. Adam noted that while the group maintained a brave face, she privately realized the risks were no longer theoretical.

Following the incident, SpaceX closed the launch facility for four months to conduct a massive clean-up operation and reconstruct the site. The event highlighted the practical challenges accompanying futuristic space endeavors, such as residents having to wipe dust from their windows. Adam’s photograph documents this pivotal moment, marking the end of her personal adventure to space.
summary: Rhiannon Adam, a photographer selected for the dearMoon Project, took a photograph of the SpaceX Starship breaking apart during its Integrated Flight Test 1 on April 20, 2023. The image was taken from the VIP viewing area in South Padre Island, Texas, showing the dust cloud from the launchpad after the vehicle's rapid unscheduled disassembly.
author: Guardian Science

title: Alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions
content:
Medical experts say that adding other measurements and tests to the body mass index (BMI) would improve care and outcomes. They argue that an alternative to BMI could prevent misdiagnosis in millions worldwide by more accurately distinguishing healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat.

BMI has long been viewed as a blunt tool for defining obesity, raising concerns that many individuals with excess body fat are overlooked while others who are healthy receive incorrect diagnoses.
summary: Doctors state that combining body mass index with other measurements and tests more accurately distinguishes healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat. This approach could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide by addressing the limitations of using BMI alone.
author: Guardian Science

title: Pomerado Launches Platform to Convert Websites into Deterministic APIs for Agents
content:
Alan and Akshay from Pomerado, a Y Combinator F26 company, have launched a self-serve platform designed to connect AI agents to any website by converting sites into deterministic, self-healing APIs. The founders state that agents are currently limited by their ability to interact with systems rather than their intelligence, as many essential services such as airlines, banks, e-commerce platforms, and government sites lack APIs or Model Context Protocols (MCPs). Consequently, agents often rely on slow, expensive, and unreliable browser automation or computer use, which many companies ban for security and compliance reasons.

The project originated from the founders’ personal experience with using agents for daily tasks, where they encountered failures in basic workflows like booking flights. After discovering that just-in-time tool creation could solve these issues, the team, who are former employees of McKinsey and Scale AI, built Pomerado to address bottlenecks in interfacing with legacy websites and apps. The platform allows developers to create APIs for any website, including those they do not own, within minutes. Users provide a natural language description of their workflow and answer a few questions to receive an MCP in under an hour.

The technical process involves an agent opening a browser to explore the website and perform the requested task once by writing HTTP requests or a Playwright script. This initial run establishes navigation and interaction methods. The agent then uses this data to create a generalizable and repeatable API, while a separate Guardian model reviews the coding agent’s calls against guardrails. The system also runs tests with synthetic inputs to prevent overfitting, and a final publication agent ensures the integration publishes a reasonable input/output schema. Future tool calls use this deterministic MCP, typically returning results in five to 30 seconds.

Pomerado handles sites requiring authentication and two-factor authentication (2FA) through a deterministic sign-in process that prevents models from reading customer credentials. Users can store 2FA TOTP seeds or link their account to a Pomerado phone number for autofill. If future runs fail, a maintenance job is triggered to repair and improve the tool. This maintenance can fix broken steps, such as renamed buttons, add new functionality, or introduce new guardrails, such as ensuring reservation dates are in the future.

Unlike computer use, Pomerado’s MCPs are deterministic at runtime, making them faster and cheaper for repeated, high-volume tasks. The company offers both an open-source version under the MIT license and a free hosted version. Current users include a personal trainer who uses agents to prepare workouts and message clients, car dealerships connecting their Grok Bots to legacy dealer systems like CRMs and ERPs, and personal assistants integrating with various consumer websites.
summary: Pomerado Launches Platform to Convert Websites into Deterministic APIs for Agents.
author: Hacker News

title: COP31 in Antalya: Turkey and Australia cohost UN climate talks as US absent
content:
COP31, the annual United Nations climate conference, is currently underway in Antalya, Turkey, with negotiations running from November 8 to November 20. Turkey and Australia are cohosting the event, which brings together thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists. The conference is described as particularly charged due to the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and caused global economic shock waves through spiked energy prices. Additionally, this marks the second consecutive COP to take place without a formal delegation from the United States, as President Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change.

The backdrop for these negotiations is marked by significant challenges to the Paris Agreement, which was established 11 years ago with a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C above preindustrial levels. A report published in September by the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed this 1.5 °C threshold, likely within the next few years. This reality raises urgent questions regarding how to quickly cut emissions and how to finance efforts to address emissions and help the world endure the resulting damage.

Climate finance remains a central issue, with the goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. According to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024. The previous year’s agreement at COP30 included a goal to triple funding for adaptation over that period, although such funding has remained flat in recent years. The stakes of these financial and environmental challenges were highlighted earlier this year by a glacier collapse in the Himalayas that caused devastating flooding, killing approximately 1,500 people, leaving over 5,000 missing, and causing nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to help Nepal recover, which is less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country.

Fossil fuels are expected to be a major point of contention, with the final agreement text from three years ago explicitly calling for a transition away from them. Last year’s agreement, however, did not mention the phrase “fossil fuels” at all. This topic is sensitive for the cohosts, as Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.

Outside of formal negotiations, COP31 president and Turkey’s environment minister, Murat Kurum, is spearheading a side agenda featuring two informal initiatives. One initiative is a pledge to make AI more sustainable, which explicitly states that it creates no new obligations for countries. The second initiative aims to increase the share of electricity in global energy use, targeting 35% of total energy consumption by 2035, up from the current 23%. While leadership bills the event as an “implementation COP,” the author notes that no groundbreaking outcomes are expected, though the final agreement will be closely watched.
summary: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: China’s Nvidia Honeypot: Jensen Huang Falls for Sexpionage Scheme
content: China’s use of sexpionage is a well‑established intelligence tactic, with recent high‑profile examples. The article notes that the world’s most powerful AI executive, Jensen Huang, fell for this approach.
summary: China has used sexpionage as a well-established intelligence tactic with recent high‑profile examples. Jensen Huang, the world’s most powerful AI executive, fell for the scheme.
author: Wired

title: AO3 Shutdown Sparks Conflict Between Readers and Authors Over Unauthorized Mirror Uploads
content: A Heated Rivalry fanfic author expressed frustration after discovering her work uploaded to AO3 mirror sites without her consent, saying it left a sour taste in her mouth.
summary: A Heated Rivalry fanfic author says the AO3 shutdown has left a sour taste in her mouth. She found her work uploaded to AO3 mirror sites without her consent.
author: Wired

title: Sony's PlayStation Pulse headset features planar magnetic drivers at $99.99
content:
Sony’s new PlayStation Pulse headset, priced at $99.99, offers a solid wireless gaming experience without the full‑spectrum feature overload that many headsets promise. The design focuses on delivering the basics well, providing good sound quality and enough extras to work with devices beyond the PlayStation 5.

Inside the headset’s unassuming ear cups are custom planar magnetic drivers that produce clean, detailed audio. The sound is neither bass‑heavy nor overly shrill, and the default equalizer setting is described as pleasing. These attributes make the Pulse a practical choice for gamers and music listeners who value quality sound without unnecessary bells and whistles.
summary: Sony's new PlayStation Pulse headset costs $99.99 and offers good sound quality. The headset contains custom planar magnetic drivers that deliver clean, detailed sound and a pleasing default equalizer.
author: The Verge

title: Google DeepMind launches AlphaGenome 2 AI to map DNA changes across cell types
content:
Google DeepMind has introduced AlphaGenome 2, an artificial‑intelligence model that seeks to explain how genetic variations influence the behavior of individual cell types. The new system is intended to give researchers a more detailed view of a complex problem that could reveal disease mechanisms and suggest new therapeutic avenues.

AlphaGenome 2 follows last year’s AlphaGenome model. While every human cell contains the same DNA, different cell types—such as heart muscle cells, skin cells, and immune cells—activate distinct sets of genes. The model aims to map how these gene‑activation patterns can shift in response to DNA changes.
summary: Google DeepMind researchers unveiled AlphaGenome 2, an AI model that predicts how DNA variations influence different cell types. The system builds on the AlphaGenome model released last year and aims to give scientists detailed insight into disease mechanisms and potential treatments.
author: The Verge

title: Zelda Notes App Helps Player Find Golden Skulltulas in Ocarina of Time Remake
content:
The author explains that hunting for Golden Skulltulas in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was never a priority. They note the game contains 100 Skulltulas spread across Hyrule, yet they cannot recall finding all of them during many hours with the original N64 title.  

When playing the Ocarina of Time remake, the author expected to ignore the Skulltulas again. Instead, while exploring Nintendo’s Zelda Notes companion app, they discovered that the app’s maps provide a useful tool for tracking down every golden spider and virtually all other collectibles in the game.  

As a result, the author now regularly opens the Zelda Notes app to verify that they have not missed any items, finding the companion app a valuable aid to completing the game’s collectible list.
summary: The author discovered that the Zelda Notes companion app’s maps help track Golden Skulltulas and other collectibles in the Ocarina of Time remake. They now frequently open the app to make sure they haven’t missed any items.
author: The Verge

title: Sharge sells Pixel 140W GaN MacBook charger for $69.90, over 25% off
content:
Sharge’s eye‑catching MacBook charger is now available at more than a 25 percent discount. The Pixel 140W GaN charger is listed on Amazon for $69.88 and on Sharge’s own site for $69.90, a $24 reduction from its usual price. The charger delivers up to 140 W of power through a single USB‑C port, and Sharge claims it can bring a 16‑inch MacBook Pro from a flat battery to 50 percent in just 25 minutes.  

The Pixel 140 is 47 percent smaller than the MacBook’s included charging brick, making it a convenient option for travelers or those with limited bag space. A pixel display on the side shows the current charging wattage and offers configurable brightness and orientation.  

Sharge also offers a 67‑W version for $19.90, a $30 discount, and a 100‑W version for $59.90, a $16 discount. These lower‑wattage models keep the same compact design and display features, appealing to users who do not need the full 140 W output.  

Other promotions highlighted in the same announcement include a Mattel Brick Shop Warthog set for $62.99, a Lenovo Yoga Mini desktop for $599.99, and a DJI Osmo Mobile 8 gimbal for $89, but the focus remains on the discounted Pixel 140W charger.
summary: Sharge sells Pixel 140W GaN MacBook charger for $69.90, over 25% off.
author: The Verge

title: Google Launches Tabletop AI Tool for Custom Collaborative Hubs
content:
Google has introduced Tabletop, a new experimental AI tool designed to generate customized collaborative hubs for coordinating with family and friends. The platform is distinct from tabletop gaming and shares visual similarities with workplace management applications like Asana and Monday. Its primary feature is a built-in AI capability that allows users to “vibecode” personalized interactive tools simply by describing them.

Users can create specific applications such as savings trackers, chore charts, and event plans. According to Google, individuals can add links, files, and ideas to the platform and then prompt the @tabletop feature or select a starter template. This process generates custom interactive tools, including trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters, and tournament brackets.
summary: Google Launches Tabletop AI Tool for Custom Collaborative Hubs.
author: The Verge

title: EU Targets Loot Boxes, Influencer Marketing in New Digital Fairness Act
content:
The European Union Commission published a proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) on Wednesday, introducing sweeping rules for gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms. The legislation aims to make online experiences fairer by targeting practices that exploit consumers into spending more time and money. Specific measures address misleading prices or availability, addictive design features such as gaming loot boxes, and undisclosed influencer marketing.

In a news bulletin, the EU Commission stated that the Act will protect consumers of all ages who shop or browse for goods and services online. The proposal seeks to curb exploitative digital practices across various platforms to ensure a more equitable online environment for users.
summary: The EU Commission has proposed the Digital Fairness Act to regulate gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms. The act targets misleading prices, addictive features such as loot boxes, and undisclosed influencer marketing to protect consumers of all ages.
author: The Verge

title: IBM to offer access to dual-processor quantum system in 2027
content:
IBM updated its quantum computing roadmap at this week’s Quantum Developer’s Conference, stating an aim to develop error-corrected quantum computers before the end of the decade. The company expanded the scope of its next-generation Nighthawk general-use processors by introducing a version featuring over 500 programmable qubits. Additionally, IBM revised its plan for linking multiple Nighthawk processors, reducing the intended number of linked systems from nine to two.

While the total number of qubits planned for next year remains unchanged, the method for achieving this target has shifted. IBM announced it will offer access to a dual-processor quantum system in 2027, reflecting the adjusted strategy for connecting its hardware.
summary: IBM announced at its Quantum Developer's Conference that it will offer access to a dual-processor quantum system in 2027. The company will expand its next‑generation Nighthawk processors to include a version with over 500 programmable qubits while reducing the planned linked systems from nine to two, keeping the total qubit count for next year unchanged.
author: Ars Technica

title: Apple to close its 28‑year‑old Support Community forum on Nov. 20, 2026
content:
Apple has announced that its long‑running online community forum will close on November 20, 2026. The company posted a notice to the Apple Support Community stating that the site will no longer accept new posts and will remain available only in a read‑only mode.

In the message, Apple thanked community members for contributing their time and expertise over 28 years of operation. The forum had served as a place for users to seek quick technical advice about Apple products, with most answers coming from fellow users and occasional input from Apple employees. Apple also directed users to the official Apple Support site for trusted guidance and support moving forward.
summary: Apple announced that the Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026 and will become read‑only with no new posts. The 28‑year‑old forum let users—and occasionally Apple employees—share technical advice about Apple products.
author: Ars Technica

title: Indie Games Jury Declines to Vote for Any Game Using Generative AI After Big Walk Reveal
content: The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game. This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance "declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity." Noting "a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools," the group of jurors called out AI's ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still "not a foregone conclusion in our industry." Read full article Comments
summary: Indie Games Jury Declines to Vote for Any Game Using Generative AI After Big Walk Reveal.
author: Ars Technica

title: Appeals court blocks Trump administration's request for journalists' LinkedIn messages
content:
An appeals court ruled that the Department of Justice’s effort to obtain 18 months of LinkedIn communications from targeted journalists was overly broad. The DOJ had asked LinkedIn to provide data from journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on a wide range of topics during that period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report about a news outlet that President Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country; the outlet is not named.

The DOJ’s request cast a wide net, seeking LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted. LinkedIn argued that allowing the request would harm the targeted journalists and undermine a platform where reporters frequently connect with confidential sources. The judges agreed.

The administration also secured a secrecy order that barred LinkedIn from telling anyone about the sweeping request for a year, leaving journalists unaware of the potential First Amendment implications. The court found that this secrecy order was problematic.
summary: An appeals court ruled that the Justice Department’s request for 18 months of LinkedIn communications from a broad group of journalists exceeded the scope of its leak investigation. The court also struck down a secrecy order that had barred LinkedIn from disclosing the request, finding it threatened journalists’ First Amendment rights.
author: Ars Technica

title: TSMC to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI
content:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSMC) has received board approval to invest up to $1 billion in two leading artificial‑intelligence developers. The plan allocates $500 million to purchase OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to buy common shares of Anthropic at the price expected for its initial public offering, according to Reuters.

The investment follows TSMC’s strong earnings from its contract chipmaking business, which has benefited from the expansion of AI data centers. The Wall Street Journal noted that the funding could provide markets with “a shot of confidence” as the AI trade shows signs of strain, while analysts cautioned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers and customers complicates the assessment of genuine demand for AI‑related hardware and services.
summary: TSMC's board approved up to $500 million for OpenAI preferred stock and $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at its expected IPO price. The investment gives the Taiwanese chipmaker direct stakes in the AI developers while its contract chipmaking business profits from AI data‑center growth.
author: Ars Technica

title: NASA announces extensive lunar contract awards at weekend news conference
content:
Senior NASA officials conducted an extensive news conference last weekend in which they announced a succession of lunar‑related contract awards and upcoming opportunities. The briefings covered landers, nuclear‑powered rovers, scouting drones, power‑generation and storage systems, and communication satellites, outlining the agency’s next steps for the Moon Base program.

During the more‑than‑90‑minute session, Moon Base Program manager Carlos García‑Galán said the pace of solicitations is intended to keep industry “on their toes” and to meet the timeline the agency has set for establishing a lunar base.
summary: Senior NASA officials held a lengthy news conference last weekend, laying out a series of lunar contract awards, new contract opportunities, and mission decisions. They followed one after the other: landers, nuclear-powered rovers, scouting drones, power generation, storage, and communication satellites.
author: Ars Technica

title: Anduril's Anduril-216 satellite demo tracks spacecraft in orbital night
content:
Anduril Industries announced that its first satellite, Anduril‑216, successfully demonstrated a new sensor capable of tracking other spacecraft that may conceal maneuvers in Earth’s shadow. The oven‑sized satellite, funded with Anduril’s internal capital, launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission in July carrying a tech‑demo payload that includes an edge‑compute processor, a power‑management system adaptable to different missions, and a long‑wave infrared sensor designed to see objects in orbit.

Anduril reported the success of the demonstration on Tuesday. Anduril‑216 operates at roughly 590 km (366 mi) altitude and spends about one‑third of each orbit in darkness, allowing its infrared imager to function during night passes.
summary: Anduril Industries said its oven‑sized satellite Anduril‑216 successfully demonstrated a long‑wave infrared sensor that can track other spacecraft maneuvering in Earth’s shadow. The SpaceX rideshare‑launched satellite, orbiting about 590 km and spending roughly one‑third of each pass in darkness, also carried an edge‑compute processor and a versatile power‑management system.
author: Ars Technica

title: T‑Mobile to remove 50 GB cap and speed limits on low‑income home internet after NY settlement
content:
T‑Mobile was found to have breached a New York state law by placing a 50‑gigabyte‑per‑month data cap and throttling speeds to less than one megabit per second on the wireless home‑Internet service it must provide to low‑income households. State officials said the limits violated the New York Affordable Broadband Act.

The company has agreed to a settlement that requires it to remove both the data cap and the speed restrictions, to broaden the availability of the low‑income plans to additional regions of the state, and to make information about the plans more accessible to consumers. The settlement obligates T‑Mobile to eliminate the speed limits and expand plan coverage within 120 days.

Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James announced the agreement on Monday, noting that a state investigation confirmed the violation. The settlement applies only to T‑Mobile’s wireless home‑Internet service and does not affect its mobile phone plans.
summary: T‑Mobile to remove 50 GB cap and speed limits on low‑income home internet after NY settlement.

content: “There are a lot of senior people in the industry that know this is happening, and are effectively condoning it,” an investment intel consultant said.

title: CoreWeave seeks upfront payments and short‑term contracts to fund AI growth
content: CoreWeave disclosed in its third‑quarter earnings that it is increasingly requiring customers to pay upfront, borrowing against specific contracts, and exploring short‑term deals that could result in higher prices. The company is using these prepayments and shorter contracts to fund its AI growth.
summary: CoreWeave is increasingly asking customers to pay upfront and borrowing against specific contracts. The company is also looking at short‑term deals that could lead to higher prices, according to its third‑quarter earnings.

title: Olaf Sakkers bets he can beat the emerging-manager squeeze
content: Olaf Sakkers, a first‑time venture‑capital fund manager, says he is betting he can beat the emerging‑manager squeeze. He notes that entering venture capital has never been easy, and that the current environment is especially daunting, but points to five years of experience that he says proves difficulty does not mean impossible.
summary: Olaf Sakkers is betting he can beat the emerging-manager squeeze. He has spent the past five years proving that difficult doesn’t mean impossible.

title: Many announced data center projects may never be built amid opposition
content: The data‑center expansion is confronting tangible hurdles, including widespread local opposition, permitting delays and competition for electricity. Even before those issues arise, a fundamental concern is that many announced projects may never be constructed, despite the billions of dollars being pledged for AI infrastructure.
summary: The data center boom is encountering obstacles such as widespread local opposition, permitting delays and a scramble for electricity. A basic problem is that many of the announced projects may never be built.

title: Rockstar North used Miami field trips since 2015 to craft GTA VI’s detailed world
content: The developers behind its virtual Florida share how they built their most ambitious world so far • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North took their first trips to Miami to do field research for the next game in the phenomenally popular crime series. “Before you’re doing hyper-organised research trips, you’re immersing yourself in the place and its history, the vibe of it,” Rob Nelson, one of the lead developers on GTA VI, tells me. “[You see] the physical places you want to move characters through, the experiences you want them to have, and the juxtaposition between the extremes of society that are in Miami.” I wondered: did people ever recognise them on any of their research trips? Did locals know what they were doing? This is the biggest game in the world, after all; I imagine it would be difficult to go entirely undercover. “We’re always semi-undercover,” he says. “But if you have a bunch of dorks going through a terrifying neighbourhood, you do stick out a bit.”
summary: In 2015, a group of Grand Theft Auto developers from Rockstar North made field research trips to Miami for the next game in the series. Lead developer Rob Nelson said the team immersed themselves in the city’s history and vibe, observing physical locations and societal extremes while working semi‑undercover.
author: Guardian Technology

title: 37 top UK Christmas gifts for tweens chosen by 10‑12‑year‑olds
content:
A recent survey of twenty tweens aged 10 to 12 across the UK asked them to list items they already own, love, and would recommend as gifts. The children highlighted classic playthings such as Lego sets and dance mats, as well as a growing interest in personal care products like lotions and potions.

The responses reflected a split in interests. Some tweens remain engaged with crafting, board games, and building with Lego, while others have shifted toward skincare routines and learning to play instruments such as the guitar.

Based on these insights, the article presents a range of gift ideas that span different price points, aiming to satisfy the diverse preferences of teenagers in the tweenage years.
summary: The article lists 37 Christmas gift ideas for tweens in the UK, based on responses from 20 children aged 10 to 12. The surveyed tweens highlighted items they already own and love, such as Lego, dance mats, skincare products and guitars.
author: Guardian Technology

title: US soldier arrested in England on suspicion of spying for Russia
content: The FBI says the case is of “the utmost concern” to Washington and its allies, while army counterintelligence chiefs warn that insider threats are “real and persistent”.
summary: US soldier arrested in England on suspicion of spying for Russia.

title: Iranian women join IRGC military training in Tehran
content:
Iranian women recently participated in a military training course organized by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) at a volunteer camp in Tehran.  

During the course, the participants handled firearms and practiced rappelling and ziplining.
summary: Iranian women participated in a military training course organized by the IRGC at a volunteer camp in Tehran. The training included handling firearms and practising rappelling and ziplining.

title: Singulus Technologies signs €60 million contract with Elon Musk’s SpaceX for satellite solar cells
content: SpaceX has signed a €60 million contract with German mechanical‑engineering firm Singulus Technologies to supply solar cells for its satellites. The agreement is described as a strategic partnership and is expected to give Singulus a significant price increase.
summary: SpaceX signed a €60 million deal with German mechanical engineering company Singulus Technologies to supply solar cells. The agreement is a strategic supply for satellite solar cells and gives Singulus a massive price jump.

title: France's Unprecedented Supermarket Refrigerator Hacks Make It Europe's Most Hacked Country
content: The “unprecedented” hacks of French supermarket refrigerators have joined a series of major cyberattacks, making France the most hacked country in Europe, analysts say. Cyberattacks are rising worldwide, yet France remains a frequent target.
summary: The hacks of French supermarket refrigerators were described as unprecedented and are part of a series of major cyberattacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe, according to some analysts. Cyberattacks are rising globally, and the article questions why France is such a ready target.
author: France 24

title: Italian schools evacuated after hoax bomb threats, PM Meloni says no concrete danger
content: Schools were evacuated across Italy on Wednesday following a series of hoax bomb threats, but Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said there was no "concrete danger". Similar hoax threats were reported in schools in Britain and Ireland, which reportedly prompted some evacuations in Scotland. Meloni said she had called a government meeting with security and intelligence chiefs for Wednesday to discuss the threats. FRANCE 24's Emerald Maxwell reports.
summary: Schools across Italy were evacuated on Wednesday after a series of hoax bomb threats. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said there was no concrete danger and called a government meeting with security and intelligence chiefs to discuss the threats.
author: France 24

title: Tens of thousands gather in Warsaw for Independence Day march days after Krakow shooting
content:
Tens of thousands of Polish nationalist sympathizers gathered in Warsaw on Wednesday for the annual Independence Day March, held just days after a deadly shooting spree in Krakow. The event takes place each November 11 to commemorate the end of 123 years of partition by Russia, Prussia, and Austria in 1918.

The march serves as a gathering point for various factions within Poland's right wing, including conservative-nationalists aligned with the Law and Justice (PiS) party, as well as far-right and radical groups. The event was covered by FRANCE 24’s Carys Garland.
summary: Tens of thousands of Polish nationalist sympathisers gathered in Warsaw on Wednesday for the annual Independence Day March. The march took place days after a deadly shooting spree in Krakow and draws participants from across Poland's right wing, including groups aligned with the Law and Justice party.
author: France 24

title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Linked to China Spy Allegations Over Chip Smuggling
content:
China has accused Nvidia of having a vulnerability at its core that could be exploited, according to the report. The allegation comes amid scrutiny of the company’s operations in China, where the firm dominates more than two‑thirds of the world’s AI computing power production.

Nvidia co‑founder Jensen Huang has admitted to an extramarital affair with Singapore‑based Chinese tech CEO Alice Huang—who is not related to him. Huang is currently under investigation for purchasing Nvidia’s latest chips, which authorities suspect may have been smuggled back to mainland China illegally.

The article will explore the rise and possible fall of the Taiwan‑born AI icon, examining how these controversies could impact his standing in the industry.
summary: China accuses Nvidia of exploiting a vulnerability involving the purchase of state‑of‑the‑art chips that may have been smuggled back to mainland China. Jensen Huang admits an extramarital affair with Singapore‑based Chinese tech CEO Alice Huang, who is under scrutiny for the chip purchase.
author: France 24

title: Reporters Without Borders calls for release of French reporter Christophe Gleizes in Algeria
content: After being detained for almost 500 days in Algeria, Christophe Gleizes is no closer to being freed. Those close to him, as well as his fellow sports journalists have campaigned tirelessly for his release with the affair even attracting the attention of Zinedine Zidane, manager of the French football team. FRANCE 24's Mark Owen speaks with Thibault Bruttin, Director General of Reporters Without Borders. He says that Gleizes has probably become "a token in a diplomatic game that we don't totally understand, that we don't totally master, up to the point where we are asking ourselves 'has he become a state hostage?'".
summary: Christophe Gleizes has been detained in Algeria for almost 500 days and remains unreleased. Reporters Without Borders' Director General Thibault Bruttin said he may have become a diplomatic hostage, as fellow journalists and football manager Zinedine Zidane have campaigned for his freedom.
author: France 24

title: France bans Samaria Regional Council head Yossi Dagan from entering country
content: French authorities compelled Yossi Dagan, head of the Samaria Regional Council, to leave France after he arrived at a Paris airport last week, his office said in a statement on Wednesday. The French foreign ministry did not confirm that he was deported, but said Dagan is banned from French territory because of his involvement in Israel’s illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank. The ministry’s comment linked the ban directly to his settlement activities.
summary: French authorities forced Samaria Regional Council head Yossi Dagan to leave France after he landed at a Paris airport last week. The French foreign ministry said Dagan is banned from French territory because of his involvement in Israel's illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, without confirming his deportation.
author: France 24

title: 17-year-old Gladbach forward Wael Mohya earns first Germany call-up
content: At 17, Gladbach forward Wael Mohya has earned his first call‑up to the German national team. The dual‑national player has opted to follow the DFB route for now and, according to the announcement, could soon set a modern national‑team record.
summary: Wael Mohya, a 17-year-old Gladbach forward, has earned his first call-up to the Germany national team. The dual‑national talent has chosen the DFB path and could soon make modern national‑team history.
author: DW World

title: AIIB grievance mechanism faces hurdles, critics call for reforms
content: The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) operates a grievance redress mechanism intended for individuals and communities impacted by its financed projects. However, the source notes that filing a complaint involves significant hurdles, prompting critics to call for reforms and greater transparency in the process.
summary: The AIIB has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. Critics say those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles and that reforms and greater transparency are needed.

title: Brazil electoral court fines Meta, finds no deliberate election bias
content: Brazil’s electoral court imposed a fine on Meta after a complaint was filed by President Luiz Inácio Lula’s coalition. The court said it found no evidence that Meta intended to influence the election. Meta responded that it will contest the charge, calling the allegations false.
summary: Brazil's electoral court fined Meta after President Lula's coalition filed a complaint, but said there was no evidence of intent to influence the election. Meta said it will defend itself against false allegations.
author: DW World

title: Australian PM Anthony Albanese omits fossil fuels in UN climate summit speech
content:
During a historic address at the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese emphasized that governments have a “solemn responsibility” to act on climate change. He highlighted Australia’s progress in renewable energy but did not mention the fossil fuels that are driving the crisis.

The speech drew criticism for overlooking the country’s large coal industry. Albanese arrived in Antalya on Wednesday morning, where COP31 is being hosted by Turkey and presided over by his climate change minister, Chris Bowen.
summary: Australian PM Anthony Albanese omits fossil fuels in UN climate summit speech.
author: Guardian World

title: Finland's Canberra embassy Instagram staff‑training post goes viral
content: Finland’s embassy in Canberra was temporarily closed on Tuesday, a move that reportedly upset millions of people worldwide. After a promotion for a “Finnish Dinner Date” gained modest online attention, the embassy’s next Instagram post – showing a staff training day – unexpectedly went viral, surprising the diplomatic team.
summary: The Finnish embassy in Canberra shared a staff‑training‑day video on Instagram that attracted widespread attention. The embassy was temporarily closed on Tuesday, prompting upset among millions of people worldwide.
author: Guardian World

title: First Covid lockdowns, then alcohol to your door: rise in young Victorians with liver diseases prompts fears
content:
Young Victorians are drinking less overall, yet a small minority are consuming large, damaging amounts of alcohol, an expert notes. This trend has coincided with a rise in hospitalisations for severe, irreversible liver disease among young people, while alcohol‑related admissions remain above pre‑pandemic levels even after peaking during Covid lockdowns.

A new report from the Burnet Institute, commissioned by the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education (Fare), analysed nearly two decades of Victorian health data. The study examined the prevalence of alcohol‑associated harm, highlighting the growing concern over liver disease in younger populations.
summary: First Covid lockdowns, then alcohol to your door: rise in young Victorians with liver diseases prompts fears.
author: Guardian World

title: David Walliams removed from Australian film and publicity after harassment allegations
content:
Transmission Films, the distributor of the upcoming Australian fantasy film Fing!, has announced that David Walliams will be removed from the movie and its publicity campaign. Walliams, a children’s author and comedian who co‑wrote the film based on his own book, will no longer appear in the film or participate in media events ahead of its 14 January cinema debut.

The decision follows sexual‑harassment allegations that were made public. Walliams was accused of using his celebrity status to prey on young women for sex, prompting the distributors to cut his cameo and withdraw him from promotional activities.

The film’s release will proceed without Walliams’ involvement, and the company has confirmed that no further appearances or marketing appearances will be scheduled for him.
summary: The distributors of an upcoming Australian film based on a book by David Walliams said he will be removed from the movie. Transmission Films confirmed he will also not participate in the film’s media campaign before its 14 January cinema debut.
author: Guardian World

title: California Democrats ask Trump admin about detained 8‑year‑old Haitian boy in San Diego
content:
Democratic lawmakers in California are pressing the Trump administration for information about an eight‑year‑old Haitian boy who was placed in restraints and taken into federal immigration custody after arriving for an immigration check‑in in San Diego. The officials say the child was led away by three armed officers following a routine appointment, according to a video obtained by NBC News.

The lawmakers are seeking answers regarding the boy’s safety and current location, noting that the incident occurred on 4 November when the family said the check‑in was a standard immigration appointment. The request for clarification comes after the video showed the third‑grader being escorted by the officers.
summary: California Democrats ask Trump admin about detained 8‑year‑old Haitian boy in San Diego.

title: Ecuadorian journalist Tomás Beltrán shot dead while parking his car amid gang violence
content:
Tomás Beltrán was shot dead while maneuvering his car into his garage on Sunday night. The Ecuadorian journalist had run a Facebook page that reported news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí.

Beltrán’s killing occurred amid gang warfare that has turned Ecuador into one of Latin America’s most violent countries. Calceta’s Pacific coastline makes it a key flashpoint in the gang conflict over drug‑trafficking routes.
summary: Tomás Beltrán, an Ecuadorian journalist who ran a Facebook page about Calceta in Manabí, was shot dead while manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night. The killing occurred amid gang warfare over drug‑trafficking routes that has turned Ecuador into one of Latin America’s most violent countries.

title: Argentinian lawyer Marcelo Kohen mocks UK historic sovereignty claim over Falklands waters
content: Argentinian lawyer Marcelo Kohen, who is representing Argentina at an international tribunal in Hamburg, criticized the United Kingdom’s claim that the British Crown holds historic sovereignty over parts of the oceans surrounding the Falkland Islands. Kohen said Britain is wrong to rely on a “historic doctrine” that treats those waters as a Dominium maris Britannici, likening the approach to a 17th‑century colonial power. Argentina told the tribunal that the UK should not be permitted to act on that doctrine in the ongoing Falklands oil case.
summary: Marcelo Kohen, an Argentine lawyer representing Argentina at a hearing in Hamburg, mocked the United Kingdom’s claim that the British crown holds historic sovereignty over waters around the Falkland Islands. He said Britain should not act as a 17th‑century colonial power treating those waters as a Dominium maris Britannici.
author: Guardian World

title: Former Red Brigades member Leonardo Bertulazzi escapes house arrest in Argentina
content:
Leonardo Bertulazzi, a 74‑year‑old former member of Italy’s Red Brigades, escaped house arrest in Buenos Aires, Argentina, according to the country’s security ministry. The ministry said Bertulazzi hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork, used a harness and lowered himself from a fifth‑floor balcony.

Bertulazzi has been awaiting extradition to Italy, where he is slated to serve a 27‑year prison term imposed in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group. Argentine authorities placed him under house arrest in 2024 pending the extradition.
summary: Former Red Brigades member Leonardo Bertulazzi escapes house arrest in Argentina.
author: Guardian World

title: Watch: Vinícius Jr's surprise message to boy who received prosthetic legs after Sudan drone strike
content: Real Madrid forward Vinícius Jr sent a surprise video message to 13‑year‑old fan Zaher, who lost both legs when a drone struck him in Khartoum in 2024. Zaher has since been fitted with prosthetic legs, and the player’s message was recorded to acknowledge the boy’s situation.
summary: Real Madrid player Vinícius Jr sent a surprise message to 13-year-old fan Zaher who lost both his legs after being hit by a drone in Khartoum, in 2024.

title: 11-month-old baby found buried alive in crate near father's home in South Carolina
content: Officials in South Carolina said an 11‑month‑old baby who had been missing was discovered buried alive in a crate near his father’s home on Tuesday, a day after he was taken. The child is currently receiving care in a hospital.
summary: Officials said the missing 11-month-old baby was found buried alive in a crate close to his father's home on Tuesday. He was found a day after he was taken and is now being cared for in a hospital.
